title: Review sequential awaits inside loops
why: Starting independent asynchronous work one iteration at a time can increase latency. Awaiting promises that have already started does not serialize their execution; ordering, backpressure, or isolated measurements may require sequential awaits.
suggestion: Use bounded concurrency only when iterations start independent work. Keep intentional ordering and backpressure; Promise.all aggregates promises but does not itself impose a concurrency limit.
limitations: Only lines beginning with await inside recognized braced loops are reported, with nested callback boundaries respected.

Infinite while (true) and bare empty-header for (;;) service loops, for-await stream consumers, explicit wait/backoff/delay/pause/sleep and direct setTimeout calls, and direct once imports or const destructuring requires from events/node:events are excluded as sequential wait/backpressure contexts. Whitespace and comments are masked normally; initialized or updating for headers do not gain this service-loop classification.

Other dependencies, ordering requirements and rate limits remain advisory review decisions. Event-wait suppression requires a real lexical import and only awaited direct uses outside that binding; any other same-name use, including shadowing, reassignment or an indirect reference, conservatively disables suppression throughout the file. Namespace aliases and arbitrary wrappers are not resolved. A nested finite loop is reviewed independently of an enclosing service loop; repeated evidence is grouped per file.

Simple awaited Promise executors that directly schedule their resolver through an unshadowed bare setTimeout or setImmediate call are recognized across lines, including a single-statement block and Promise type arguments. Delay calculations are not profiled. Other callbacks, additional executor statements, chained continuations, shadowed runtime names and unresolved timer imports or namespace aliases do not gain this proof. Type-only timer references and unrelated object methods do not shadow the global scheduler. A timer name inside a string or an unrelated call is not wait evidence.

Direct calls to unique same-file module-level timer helpers are recognized only when their returned Promise uses one known scheduler and no other call targets beyond resolution, cancellation and a local abort handler on a conventional AbortSignal parameter. Rebound or indirect helper references, unknown callbacks, extra work and unsupported invocation syntax retain advice; arbitrary logging and retry wrappers are not inferred.

A bounded shared-cursor pool is recognized when a zero-argument async worker claims an index before awaiting the corresponding item callback, Array.from launches Math.min(cap, items.length) workers, and Promise.all immediately joins the resulting pool. Cursor reuse, extra worker references, mismatched items, unjoined pools and replaced runtime bindings retain advice. Only the matched worker await is excluded, not neighboring loops.

A direct semicolon-terminated awaited call is excluded when only straight-line call statements lead to an unconditional return within the same recognized function. An unlabeled break also qualifies only when that function contains one lexical loop keyword and no switch. Functions containing finally blocks, conditional exits, labeled or nested-loop breaks, intervening assignments, unsupported call expressions and unresolved function regions remain conservative. Retry or pagination names alone never establish this proof.

A partial-success prefix contract is recognized when a local let counter is initialized to zero immediately before a for loop, incremented unconditionally in its sole outer try, copied to that catch's error before rethrowing the same error, and returned immediately after the loop. Only awaits before the increment are excluded. Publication may be direct or inside one if guard. Extra counter references, aliases, shadows, nested functions or loops, finally clauses, early control transfers, conditional increments and later error reuse retain advice. Remote queue admission and rollback API semantics are not resolved.

A do/while stabilization barrier is recognized when a uniquely used local let snapshot is assigned a plain reference or zero-argument getter result, awaited directly or through a property, and compared with that same source using strict identity inequality. The body must contain only assignment and await; the snapshot declaration plus its three loop references must be the only uses in the recognized function. Different getters, aliasing, extra work, other conditions and unresolved bindings retain advice. Callback, stream and protocol names alone do not prove serialization.

Collecting already-started promises does not start additional parallel work; benchmark isolation, shared graph traversal, protocol framing and wrapper-based stream waits can also require serialization. These remain contextual advice unless a recognized sequential form proves the intent.
